content:
Outside support will not show up because you hoped for it. You ask for it. You go to personal contacts and partner churches, name a specific amount, and tie that amount to the church budget. A coach can review the plan. A sending church can open a door. Neither one makes the requests for you.

That money is not a score of your Core Group. A partner gift can fund a launch while the core is still learning to give. A sacrificial core can still leave the budget short. You raise the outside portion the budget needs, and you leave every gift record with the Financial Leader.

---

## You make the request

You lead the asks. You approach personal contacts and partner churches with a specific funding request. The Financial Leader receives the gift and keeps the books.

A sending church, a coach, or a network office may suggest a name. They do not make the requests. If a network or foundation invites an application, you complete it yourself. You do not give them the church's giving records.

Do not start until you have a Financial Leader. A request with no receiver puts the check in your hand. [Principles of Financial Accountability](/wiki/administrative/financial/principles-of-financial-accountability) already says the Senior Pastor does not handle money, write checks, or know individual giving amounts. This guide does not move that line.

---

## Tie every ask to the budget

Build the first-year budget with your coach before you call anyone. [First Year Budget Planning](/wiki/administrative/financial/first-year-budget-planning) is where you set categories, the local giving estimate, and outside support as one income source. Use those numbers. Do not keep a more hopeful set for the calls.

Write three figures.

- Core Group commitments already in hand, as one total.
- The remaining gap for the period the budget covers.
- The lines that gap will pay, including compensation, rent, and other operating costs.

Ask for one line, or a stated share of the gap, with a dollar amount and an end date. "Help if you can" is not a request. Neither is a round number you have not tied to the budget.

Count only an agreement you can repeat to the Financial Leader. A warm conversation is not income. Change the budget when a commitment changes. Do not spend a gift that has not arrived.

<Callout type="important">
IRS Publication 526 for 2025, checked October 26, 2026, says a payment to a member of the clergy that they can spend as they wish is not a deductible contribution. Ask people to give to the church for the approved budget. Do not ask them to pay you, and do not promise a tax deduction. Confirm the current IRS publication before you describe a gift, and tell donors to ask their own tax adviser.
</Callout>

---

## Decide who you will approach

Stay with people and churches that already have a tie to you or to this plant.

**Personal contacts.** Friends, family, and people from a church you served who know this work. Ask them to give to the church, not to sponsor you as a private project.

**Partner churches.** A sending church, or a church whose leaders have said they want to help a plant. Ask the pastors or elders. A written request uses the same line, amount, dates, and church legal name you would say out loud.

Do not run a mass appeal, and do not ask for the Core Group giving list so you can judge who can afford more.

Do not pay anyone, including yourself, a percentage of what is raised. The church sets compensation in the budget and pays it through payroll. A gift is not a commission.

<Callout type="warning">
One clear ask is enough. If they need time, follow up once, on the date you agreed. If they say no, thank them and stop. Do not push a gift that would strain their household or their church. A refusal is a complete answer.
</Callout>

---

## Make one clear request

Prepare before the conversation so you are not inventing numbers while they listen.

- [ ] Write the budget line, amount, and dates.
- [ ] Get the church legal name and the giving instructions from the Financial Leader.
- [ ] Write what the gift will pay for, and what it will not pay for.
- [ ] Pick the one follow-up date you will use if they need time.
- [ ] Leave room for a no, with no second pitch waiting.

Say how you know them. Name the need and the amount. Say the gift goes to the church. Ask whether they want to take part. Then stop talking.

Tell the truth about the plant. Do not inflate the Core Group, the launch date, or what their gift will accomplish. If you mention a past event, date it. Do what you said you would do with the money.

Accept a restriction only for a fund the elders have already established. Read [Designated Giving Policies](/wiki/administrative/financial/designated-giving-policies) before you agree, and have the Financial Leader confirm the wording. Refuse "for the planter to use as needed." The IRS tells donors they cannot deduct a gift earmarked for a specific person, even when the check is written to a qualified organization.

The Financial Leader sends the acknowledgment. You do not write it. Follow [Donor Receipts and Giving Statements](/wiki/administrative/financial/donor-receipts-and-giving-statements). A receipt is not a promise that the donor can deduct the gift.

---

## Keep the books with the Financial Leader

You will know the amount you asked for, because you named it. That knowledge is the request, not a giving report. You do not learn from the church's records who paid, who paid less, or who paid more. Do not ask. Do not open the giving software or the bank account.

If a partner says they sent the gift, thank them for partnering with the church. Do not match their words to the books. If they ask whether it arrived, send them to the Financial Leader.

If someone hands you cash or a check, leave it sealed and do not write down the amount. The same day, give it to the Financial Leader with a second person present. If the Financial Leader is away, put it unopened in the locked container your counting process already uses, with two people. Do not take it home.

The report you receive has no names.

| What you see | What you do not see |
| --- | --- |
| Outside support pledged, from your ask log | Who pledged it |
| Outside support received, as one total | Which gift arrived |
| Core Group giving, as one total | Any household amount |
| The remaining budget gap | A deposit list or donor statement |

Keep an ask log of who you asked, the amount, what they said, and any restriction. Send the Financial Leader a copy. Do not add payment results to your copy.

If you asked only one partner for a line, a received total tells you they gave. Do not ask the amount, the date, or whether they gave more. Do not use that inference when you preach, pray in public, or decide how to treat them. Where you can, point more than one partner at the same line so a total does not name a household.

---

## Separate outside support from Core Group generosity

Keep two questions apart.

**Financial readiness.** Does the church have enough, from every source in the budget, to meet the bills you approved?

**Generosity.** Are Core Group households learning to give regularly and sacrificially?

Outside support answers the first question. It does not answer the second. Report the totals separately to your coach and to the elders. Do not add partner money to the Core Group giving total.

<Callout type="insight">
A funded budget is not a generous Core Group. Outside support and Core Group giving answer different questions. Do not treat either one as proof of the other.
</Callout>

The Core Group is still assigned to give, and that giving is still the church's primary funding. Outside support covers lines those commitments do not yet cover, including operating costs. Teach the Core Group to give. Thank the group. Do not thank a household for a figure you do not have.

After launch, local giving should carry the church. [Financial Sustainability](/wiki/post-launch/financial-sustainability) describes that shift. Raise outside support now for lines in the launch budget, and plan for those gifts to taper. Do not hold budgeted work until local giving covers every line. Do not build a church that can pay its bills only if partner gifts never end.

Everyfield does not store these gifts, score generosity, or decide whether you may launch. Keep the budget, the ask log, and the gift records in the church's own financial records.

---

## Mistakes that break the boundary

**Asking for a personal gift.** "Make the check out to me" misses the church's books. Ask for an approved budget line.

**Letting someone else own the ask.** A partner can open a door. If they also hold the list and tell you who paid, you have given away the relationship and the boundary.

**Treating a maybe as cash.** Spend only what the Financial Leader says has arrived.

**Checking the books just this once.** Looking up the payment is how the pastor's gift knowledge starts. Do not start.

---

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Not that I seek the gift itself, but I seek the fruit which increases to your account."* — Philippians 4:17 (LSB)
</Callout>

Ask for what the budget needs. Then leave the gift alone.

title: Raising Outside Support

sources.claim: A payment to a pastor that the pastor can spend as they wish is not a deductible charitable contribution.
sources.quote: Payments to a member of the clergy that can be spent as they wish, such as for personal expenses.

sources.claim: Contributions to specific individuals are not deductible.
sources.quote: You can’t deduct contributions to specific individuals, including the following.

sources.claim: A gift earmarked for a specific person is not deductible even when paid to a qualified organization.
sources.quote: You can’t deduct these contributions even if you make them to a qualified organization for the benefit of a specific person.

sources.claim: Fundraising statements of fact and descriptions of financial condition must be current, complete, and accurate, without material omissions or exaggerations.
sources.quote: In securing charitable gifts, all representations of fact, descriptions of the financial condition of the organization, or narratives about events must be current, complete, and accurate.

sources.claim: An organization must honor what it tells givers their gifts will be used for, and must not create unrealistic expectations of what a gift will accomplish.
sources.quote: Statements made about the use of gifts by an organization in its charitable gift appeals must be honored.

sources.claim: Gift appeals must not create unrealistic expectations of what a gift will actually accomplish.
sources.quote: Appeals for charitable gifts must not create unrealistic expectations of what a gift will actually accomplish.

sources.claim: The organization, not the person who asked, provides timely gift acknowledgments.
sources.quote: Every organization shall provide givers appropriate and timely gift acknowledgments.

sources.claim: Do not press a giver into a commitment that would place a hardship on them.
sources.quote: An organization must make every effort to avoid knowingly accepting a gift from, or entering into a contract with, a giver that would place a hardship on the giver or place the giver’s future well-being in jeopardy.

sources.claim: Staff and fundraising help are not paid a percentage of the contributions they raise.
sources.quote: An organization may not base compensation of outside stewardship resource consultants or its own staff directly or indirectly on a percentage of charitable contributions raised.

claim_check.notes: Owner review by Sebastian; no model review per his 2026-10-26 instruction.

rulings: Bryan ruled B1 = Option B: "Planter-led support raising" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).

Wording call: title is Raising Outside Support rather than the backlog title Raising Outside Support: Your Fundraising Strategy, so the title names the ruled work. Slug kept as the brief's suggested path. Phase 0, with the other financial guides, because the asks belong with first-year budget work before launch. sort_order 10, the next unused integer in this section.

Wording call on confidentiality: Bryan's Option B ruling assigns the ask to the planter and gift receipt and the books to the Financial Leader. It did not authorize the Senior Pastor to see individual giving records. This draft keeps the published boundary in Principles of Financial Accountability. You may know the amount you requested because you named it. You do not receive gift records, payment confirmations, or household amounts. Reports are budget-line totals only. A single-partner line can reveal a payment by inference. The draft says not to chase that amount or use it when preaching, praying in public, or deciding how to treat the partner.

Wording call on how hard to ask: Bryan did not rule a repeated-ask or percentage model. This draft teaches one specific budget-line request and one follow-up if the person asked for time. A no ends the ask. No one is paid a percentage of gifts raised. The percentage limit follows ECFA Standard 7.5, fetched 2026-10-26, not a new Everyfield rule.

Wording call on primary funding: the Playbook still assigns primary funding to the Core Group. This draft does not replace that with partner funding as the ongoing base, and it does not adopt the unchosen option of a smaller launch paced mainly by local giving. Outside support is planter-led money for named launch budget lines, including operating costs, tracked apart from Core Group generosity. Local giving remains the post-launch path in Financial Sustainability. This draft does not revise the Core Group assignments article, which says no outside organization writes checks. It follows the named budget, accountability, and sustainability articles.

Applied Bryan's C06 ruling: outside support is funds available to launch, not evidence that the Core Group is giving sacrificially. Generosity and financial readiness stay separate questions, including C21's question of whether people are learning to give sacrificially.
